title: Multi-tenant QoS & Credit-aware Routing — Architecture Review Notes
body:
Context:
We reviewed the proposed RFC for tenant-level QoS enforcement and a credit-aware routing layer that integrates with billing and Reserved/Dedicated capacity pools. The goal is to provide predictable SLOs for paid tiers while preserving latency for best-effort traffic and keeping cost visibility for customers.

Problem statement:
- Increasing incidence of noisy tenants causing tail latency and capacity contention on shared pools.
- Current routing does not account for purchased credits or priority tiers; billing and billing-aware fallbacks are ad-hoc.
- Need a single, auditable decision point to enforce tenant priorities, allow short-term bursting, and provide graceful degradation paths.

Proposed design (recap):
1) Frontline request classifier (edge proxy) tags each request with tenant_id, route_policy_hint (from token metadata), and estimated token-weight (heuristic from model + prompt length).
2) Credit ledger service (read-optimized) keeps soft balances and bursting allowance. Router queries lightweight cache (TTL 500ms) to accept/reject or route to tiered pools.
3) Routing policy: weighted fair-queueing per tenant group with token-bucket shaping. Gold/silver/bronze maps to reserved capacity, soft-reserve, best-effort.
4) Fallbacks: when a tenant is credit-depleted or reserved pool saturated, options are: (a) route to lower-cost quantized model variant, (b) queue with retry/backoff up to configured timeout, (c) fail with informative error including billing UI link.
5) Observability contract: per-tenant metrics (consumption, denied requests, fallback reason), end-to-end latency breakdown (edge, routing, model-serving), and audit log entries for every credit decision.

Key tradeoffs discussed:
- Latency overhead vs correctness: synchronous credit check on every request increases P99. Mitigation: local cache + leaky-bucket preallocation at edge. Decision boundary: prefer read-mostly cache with occasional strong-consistency reconciliation rather than blocking RPC on each request.
- Complexity vs flexibility: full ledger atomicity is costly. We accepted eventual-consistency for balances with the ability to enforce hard limits in dedicated pools.
- Fairness vs simplicity: per-tenant WFQ is most fair but heavier. We considered tenant-grouping (per-customer account) as a pragmatic compromise to reduce state.

Open technical risks:
- Cache staleness causing slight overcommit in bursty workloads. Need guardrails and reconciliation frequency.
- Interaction with autoscaler: routing might constantly move load between pools causing oscillation. Throttle routing changes and prefer sticky allocations for short windows (30s).
- Billing disputes: customers may contest micro-denials caused by eventual consistency. Need clear UI messaging and replayable audit logs.

Operational considerations:
- Feature flags: gate credit checks and fallback behavior behind FF to ramp. Start with off for hostedsandbox tenants, then enable for a small cohort.
- Backpressure: if router queue grows, surface to SREs and trigger autoscaler policies only after sustained pressure.
- Migration: phase 1 read-only ledger to collect data, phase 2 soft-enforce, phase 3 hard-enforce with billing reconciliation.

Alternative approaches briefly covered:
- Centralized admission controller: easier to reason about but single point of failure and scaling concerns.
- Pure price-based throttling: simple but doesn't map to reserved capacity guarantees.
- Tokenized per-request payment: too complex for immediate rollout.

References in discussion:
- Existing prefix-KV cache design (affects how we estimate token-weight)
- Console quota UI mockups (Sofia) for denied-request UX
- Billing team’s micro-invoice schema (Jordan) for mapping credit consumption to invoice line items

Summary:
Team consensus leans toward hybrid design: local cache-backed credit checks + periodic reconciliation, group-level WFQ, and tiered fallback options (quantized model variant preferred for latency-critical traffic). We will prototype the cache and router integration and collect metrics before any hard enforcement.
decisions: Adopt hybrid credit-check model: local cache (TTL ~500ms) + eventual-consistency ledger
Implement group-level WFQ for initial rollout (per-customer grouping, not per-tenant) to reduce state
Fallback chain: prefer lower-cost model variant -> short queue with retry -> informative failure
Expose audit logs and per-tenant metrics before enabling hard enforcement
Gate rollout behind feature flags and a 3-phase migration plan (observe -> soft-enforce -> hard-enforce)

(Ethan) Add SRE playbook draft for backpressure scenarios and autoscaler knobs by 2024-11-01
